disagreements.about: whether a note outside the chord is a wrong note or the point
disagreements.position: a tension held over a chord is the most expressive note in the phrase
disagreements.settledBy: the length: a passing note is mine, a long note on the change is theirs
disagreements.theirs: at a change the note is a chord tone or the chord is something else

disagreements.about: whether the tune or the line decides where a phrase breathes
disagreements.position: the rest is in the tune, and a line written past it will not be sung as written
disagreements.settledBy: the long notes: both agree the phrase ends there, and the rest belongs to whichever is longer
disagreements.theirs: the breath is where the sentence ends, and the tune can hold a note for it

disagreements.about: whether a tune that repeats has stopped developing
disagreements.position: a figure heard three times is how a listener learns it, and the third time is not laziness
disagreements.settledBy: the section: the figure repeats inside one and changes when the form turns
disagreements.theirs: a form that never turns is a loop, and the tune repeating is part of why

disagreements.about: whether the tune and the bass may move together
disagreements.position: a tune doubling the bass an octave up has no shape of its own
disagreements.settledBy: the register and the rhythm: doubling in the same rhythm is mine to change, a shared root on a downbeat is fine
disagreements.theirs: the root is where the line goes, and the tune following it is the tune's problem

disagreements.about: whether a tune may sit off the grid
disagreements.position: a phrase breathes where the singer breathes, which is not always a step
disagreements.settledBy: the grid: the tune lands on steps, and which steps is mine
disagreements.theirs: a note off the step grid is a note nobody can play in time

disagreements.about: whether a sampled phrase counts as the tune
disagreements.position: a lifted phrase is somebody else's tune, and the song still needs one of its own
disagreements.settledBy: the clearance: a lifted tune is a source to clear, a written one is the song's
disagreements.theirs: the loop is the source and the song is built around it, tune included

disagreements.about: whether a song needs a tune at all
disagreements.position: a song with no melody is a track, and the difference is what a listener sings back
disagreements.settledBy: the stitch: a melody no section names is the Producer's to cut
disagreements.theirs: parts are counted and cut, and a tune nothing sounds is a part like any other

disagreements.about: whether a tune that disappears is a mix problem
disagreements.position: a tune buried under the chords is written in the wrong register, not mixed wrong
disagreements.settledBy: the register: if the tune shares an octave with the chords it is mine, otherwise it is theirs
disagreements.theirs: anything that cannot be heard is a fader, and the notes need not move

goldens.passes: Agreed: it sits in one voice's range, it walks, it lands, and something repeats.

goldens.passes: Agreed with a caveat: nothing is refused, and the step count is named as close to the floor. This is the tension between the lineages made visible — a tune typical of one of them sits at the edge of a threshold set by another, and the caveat is how the bible says so.
goldens.premise: A tenth as the widest leap, a bare half of the moves steps, everything landing on chord tones — a Wonder-shaped tune put to the general rules.

lineages.instrument: a tune sung before it is played
lineages.name: Paul McCartney
lineages.why: The most examined melodies in popular music, and the method reads as arithmetic: move by step almost everywhere, leap once where the phrase turns, and stay inside a range a person can actually sing. The songs are transcribed to death, so every number this bible takes from them can be checked against the page rather than against a memory of the record.

lineages.instrument: a tune played and sung at once
lineages.name: Stevie Wonder
lineages.why: The documented counter-case: wide intervals and heavy syncopation that still sing, because the leaps land on chord tones and the rhythm repeats even when the pitches do not. Without this lineage the bible would simply punish leaping, which would rule out half of the music this app is for.

lineages.name: Ennio Morricone
lineages.why: The motif as the unit of composition: a short figure stated plainly, repeated, and moved to a new degree rather than developed away. It is the closest documented practice to how loop-based music actually builds a tune, which makes it the lineage that sets the repetition floor here while the other two set the range and the leaps.

listensFor.what: Whether anyone can sing it: the range, and the widest leap in it.
Whether it lands on the chord underneath.
Whether you have heard any of it before: the figure that comes back.
Whether it breathes, and how busy it is.

name: Melodist

openQuestions.alternative: A motif is a rhythm as much as a shape — Superstition's figure repeats its rhythm while its pitches move — so the measure should be over pitch-and-duration pairs, which would count far fewer things as repeats and would need a tolerance rather than equality.
openQuestions.encoded: The longest run of intervals that occurs twice, ignoring how long the notes are.
openQuestions.question: Is a repeated interval figure the right measure of a motif, or does it miss the rhythm?

openQuestions.alternative: Range is a property of a voice, not of a tune: a trained singer carries two octaves and an instrument carries whatever it has. The ceiling should come from the take's measured register when the song has one, and only fall back to a number when it does not.
openQuestions.encoded: Nineteen, an octave and a fifth, from the McCartney range topping out near seventeen.
openQuestions.question: Is nineteen semitones the ceiling, or does it depend on who is singing?

openQuestions.alternative: A synth lead has no breath and no range, and holding a bassline-style riff to a singer's limits would rule out most of the music this app is for — the rules should read the part's instrument and relax when nothing has to breathe.
openQuestions.encoded: Yes: the same thresholds whatever plays it, on the argument that singable is memorable.

evidence.inferred: the tension between the cited lineages and this app's first idiom

openQuestions.question: Should an instrumental line be held to singable limits at all?

openQuestions.alternative: A long note held across a change is a suspension over the second chord, which is the most expressive thing a tune does — judging it only by where it started calls that correct when it may be the one note to fix, or the reverse.
openQuestions.question: Should a note be judged against the chord it starts on, or the one it is sounding over?

owns: The tune: how far it travels, how it moves between notes, how much of it repeats, whether it lands on the chord, and whether it breathes.

refusals.because: a melody is the one part of a song where an invention nobody asked for is worse than nothing, and this app's whole bargain is that the band reads and offers rather than decides
refusals.instead: say what would make it singable — the range, the leap, the figure — and let the user draw it in the Piano roll

refusals.because: the stresses and the rhymes are the Lyricist's, and a melody read as syllables is a reading of the words instead
refusals.instead: say where the long notes and the rests are, and let the Lyricist fit the line to them
refusals.refuses: saying which words go on which note

refusals.because: the progression has an owner who measures voice leading and cadence, and a melody that reharmonises silently would overrule it
refusals.instead: say which notes are not chord tones and let the Harmonist say whether the chord or the note should move
refusals.refuses: choosing the chords under the tune

refusals.because: a tune is a shape on the grid and a take is a performance of it; drift and timing have their own readers
refusals.instead: read the written melody, and let the take's critics read the singing

rules.engineAction: SongGraph.Melody.notes, a phrase transposed by MusicTheory.Pitch
rules.then: move a phrase an octave, or split it: past nineteen semitones one person cannot sing both ends of it
rules.when: a tune spans more than an octave and a half

rules.engineAction: SongGraph.Melody.notes, the interval after the leap reversed
rules.then: come back the other way by step; a leap out and a leap on is two phrases with a hole between them
rules.when: a leap is wider than an octave

rules.engineAction: SongGraph.Melody.notes, passing notes added between leaps
rules.then: walk between the leaps; a tune of only jumps is an arpeggio and nobody sings it back
rules.when: fewer than half the moves are a tone or less

rules.then: land the long notes on chord tones and pass through the rest; the Harmonist says which they are
rules.when: fewer than three in five notes belong to the chord under them

rules.engineAction: SongGraph.Melody.notes, an interval figure repeated at a new degree
rules.then: state a cell and bring it back, moved if you like; a line that never repeats is a walk
rules.when: no figure in the tune is heard twice

rules.engineAction: SongGraph.Melody.notes at the maximum MusicTheory.Pitch.midi, lowered but one
rules.then: keep the top note for once, twice at most; a ceiling touched over and over is a range, not a climax
rules.when: the highest note is struck more than three times

rules.engineAction: SongGraph.Melody.notes shortened or removed to open a rest
rules.then: leave a gap: a singer has to breathe and a listener has to hear the end of the phrase
rules.when: a tune sounds for its whole length

evidence.inferred: eight a bar is a note every eighth: past that it reads as a run

rules.then: thin it: past eight a bar the tune is a texture and nobody sings a texture back
rules.when: a bar carries more than eight notes

rules.engineAction: SongGraph.Melody left to the Piano roll's melody mode

evidence.inferred: the app's own line: the band reads and offers, the user decides

rules.then: say what would make it singable and let the user draw it; nothing in this app writes a melody, and inventing one silently would be the worst thing here to get wrong
say the notes as degrees of the key and the moves in semitones, never as MIDI numbers
move the whole thing by octaves before changing a note; the shape is the tune and the register is a decision about who sings it
rules.when: a tune sits too high or too low for a singer

examples: Eleven semitones top to bottom, mostly steps. Anyone can sing that.
The figure in bar 1 never comes back. State it again in bar 3 and it is a tune.
It never stops: every beat of four bars is sounding. Leave a beat and the phrase ends somewhere.
voice.register: Degrees and semitones, said the way a singer would feel them. Names the one interval that is the problem, and never rewrites the tune.
voice.sentenceShape: the shape, then the number — "It walks from the 5 down to the 1, then leaps a tenth. That is the one nobody can sing."
